cases.title: Abidjan: fake Canada job ads feeding a trafficking-run pyramid scam (INTERPOL)
cases.summary: In February 2025 Côte d'Ivoire's national police, acting on an investigation that began in Ghana and was coordinated by INTERPOL, raided premises in Abidjan, arrested two suspects and rescued 33 victims from Benin, Burkina Faso, Ghana and Togo. The victims had answered online job advertisements promising work in Canada, contacted through numbers that appeared Canadian, and had paid nearly US$9,000 each for supposed travel arrangements. On arrival their documents were confiscated and, under threats and abuse, they were forced to recruit further victims through multi-level-marketing platforms, posing in luxury shops and hotels to keep up the illusion of success abroad. The suspects are not named and no conviction is reported.

cases.title: Alabuga Start (Tatarstan drone factory recruitment)
cases.summary: Alabuga Start is a recruitment program promoted on social media that offers young foreign women, mostly aged 18–22 from countries including Uganda, Rwanda, Kenya, South Sudan, Sierra Leone and Nigeria, plane tickets, money and work-study roles such as hospitality and catering. According to an AP investigation, many learned only after arriving at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan that they would assemble Iranian-designed attack drones, and described long surveilled shifts, broken wage promises, and chemical exposure. The US Treasury sanctioned SEZ Alabuga in February 2024, the EU requires EU operators to withdraw from the zone, and in May 2026 the UK designated people and entities involved in recruitment for Alabuga Start.

cases.title: Bengaluru: Bangladeshi women lured with jobs via TikTok and Facebook ("TikTok Ridoy")
cases.summary: In May 2021 a video of the gang rape of a 22-year-old Bangladeshi woman in Bengaluru went viral. Police arrested 12 people, 11 of them Bangladeshi nationals who had entered India illegally, and said the ring lured young Bangladeshi women with the pretext of employment, in some cases telling them the destination was Dubai, then forced them into prostitution; the victim was assaulted for refusing sex work. The ringleader, Rifadul Islam alias "TikTok Ridoy", used a TikTok following and Facebook groups to recruit. On 20 and 21 May 2022 a special court in Bengaluru convicted eleven: seven men were sentenced to life imprisonment, one woman to 20 years, one man to five years and two women to nine months under the Foreigners Act.

cases.title: Bolaji Bolarinwa (domestic servitude, New Jersey)
cases.summary: Bolaji Bolarinwa of Moorestown, New Jersey recruited two women to come to the United States, one of them on a student visa, and then forced them to do household work and childcare in her home. According to DOJ, she lured them with false promises, confiscated their passports and used threats of physical harm (including to one victim's daughter), verbal and physical abuse, isolation and constant surveillance to make them work around the clock with minimal pay, from about December 2015 to October 2016. After a two-week trial she was found guilty of two counts of forced labor, one count of alien harboring for financial gain and two counts of document servitude. In May 2025 she was sentenced to 45 months in prison, three years of supervised release, a $35,000 fine and $87,518.72 in restitution.

cases.title: Brandon Sartor (multi-state sex trafficking)
cases.summary: Brandon Sartor of Prince George's County, Maryland initially recruited each victim by falsely promising to help them make money. From December 2024 to April 2025 he then compelled them to have sex with as many as 10 men a day across Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Maryland, Pennsylvania and South Carolina, seizing the money. cases.title: Brazil: Gisele Bündchen deepfake Instagram ads

cases.title: Two Brazilians lured by Thailand job offers into the KK Park scam compound
cases.summary: Two men from São Paulo, aged 31 and 26, accepted supposed job offers in Thailand in late 2024, one for R$8,000 a month. One was collected from a hostel in Thailand and driven across the border to the KK Park compound in Myawaddy, Myanmar, described as an online scam factory. Both were forced to work more than 15 hours a day running internet fraud and were beaten when quotas were missed. They escaped on 8 February 2025 with other migrants, were held by a local militia, and were transferred to Thailand with pressure from the NGO The Exodus Road and consular help from Brazil's embassy in Bangkok. They landed in São Paulo on 19 February 2025 and gave statements to the Federal Police. No arrests or charges are reported.

cases.summary: India's Central Bureau of Investigation registered a case in December 2025 against a network of agents accused of trafficking Indians to Southeast Asian scam compounds for "cyber slavery". cases.title: Colombia's first domestic-servitude trafficking conviction (Vaupés to Bogotá)
cases.summary: In September 2018 a Colombian court handed down the country's first conviction for trafficking in persons for domestic servitude, sentencing a Colombian woman (not named by UNODC) to 13 years and 2 months. The victim, an 18-year-old Indigenous woman from Vaupés, was promised domestic work and a salary of US$77. On arrival in Bogotá she was told she would get no pay for two months to cover her travel tickets, then another 20 months unpaid for a decorative item she had broken. She worked over 12 hours a day with restrictions on her freedom. The prosecution argued abuse of a position of vulnerability, citing a UNODC issue paper.

cases.title: Daren Li: $73.6 million pig-butchering laundering network (California)
cases.summary: US prosecutors said Daren Li, a dual national of China and St Kitts and Nevis, directed a laundering network of about 74 US shell companies and bank accounts that received the proceeds of cryptocurrency investment ("pig-butchering") scams run from scam centres in Cambodia and elsewhere in Southeast Asia, moving funds to bank accounts in the Bahamas and converting them to USDT. cases.title: Dubai: job promises used to force women into prostitution (Al Hamriya)
cases.summary: On 20 August 2020 the Dubai Criminal Court convicted seven people, four Bangladeshi citizens, a Pakistani man and two Indonesian women, of human trafficking, unlawful confinement and forcing women into prostitution in a flat in Dubai's Al Hamriya district. The case broke when a victim used an open Wi-Fi network on a phone without a SIM card to reach her sister on Facebook, and police raided the flat. The convicted are not named in the report.

cases.title: Dzaleka refugee camp trafficking network (Malawi)
cases.summary: UNODC and the Malawi Police Service report that a trafficking network used the Dzaleka Refugee Camp, 41 km from Lilongwe, as a hub. Agents in Ethiopia, the DRC and Burundi recruited people under false pretences, offering work in South Africa, and arranged their crossing into Malawi and entry into the camp; there they were told to pay off debts for being smuggled and were exploited in the camp or moved on for forced labour. Children were exploited for farm and domestic work and women and girls for sexual exploitation, in the camp, in Malawi and elsewhere in Southern Africa. After UNODC training, over 90 victims were identified and rescued, most of them Ethiopian men aged 18–30. As of May 2022 there were five arrests of suspects from Malawi, Ethiopia, Burundi, Rwanda and the DRC and cases were ongoing; police said victims' fear of testifying was hampering convictions. No one is named.

cases.title: Josephine Iyamu ("Madam Sandra"): Nigerian women trafficked to German brothels via Libya
cases.summary: Josephine Iyamu, a London-based nurse known to victims as Madam Sandra, recruited five women from rural Nigeria, bound them with a juju oath ceremony, and had them taken overland across Africa, through Libya, by boat to Italy and on to Germany on false documents, demanding €30,000 to €38,000 each to be repaid through prostitution in brothels. The UK National Crime Agency arrested her at Heathrow in August 2017. A Birmingham Crown Court jury convicted her in June 2018 of Modern Slavery Act offences and perverting the course of justice; she was sentenced to 14 years in July 2018, increased to 18 years by the Court of Appeal in September 2018. It was the first UK conviction under the Modern Slavery Act for trafficking carried out entirely abroad.

cases.title: Los Villatoros Harvesting (Mexican H-2A farmworkers)
cases.summary: Los Villatoros Harvesting (LVH), a farm labor contracting company, operated as a criminal enterprise between about 2015 and 2017. It fraudulently recruited Mexican nationals on short-term H-2A agricultural visas, charged exorbitant recruitment fees and lied about pay, hours, working conditions and expense reimbursement. In the US, workers were compelled to do long hours of farm labour six to seven days a week in Florida, Kentucky, Indiana, Georgia and North Carolina, for far less than they were owed. Coercion included imposed debts, confiscated passports, crowded and unsanitary housing, isolation, verbal abuse and threats of arrest, deportation and harm to family in Mexico. In June 2026 Alexander Villatoro Moreno was sentenced to 70 months in prison after pleading guilty to RICO conspiracy; company owner Bladimir Moreno had been sentenced to 118 months in 2022, and co-defendants received 41 months, 37 months and 8 months' home detention.

cases.summary: According to UNODC, six Nepali nationals said they had been recruited through an agent about a year earlier and set out to reach the United States via Bolivia. cases.title: Saudi Arabia: Kenyan domestic workers in forced-labour conditions (Amnesty investigation)

cases.summary: On 11 April 2026 Spain's Guardia Civil announced Operación Balarama, which freed 80 victims aged 20 to 35, mainly Nepali, Pakistani and Senegalese nationals, exploited in agricultural harvesting in the provinces of Castellón and Valencia. cases.title: Operation Fort: Polish forced-labour ring in the West Midlands (UK)
cases.summary: Operation Fort, led by West Midlands Police with National Crime Agency support, is described by the UK government as the largest case prosecuted under UK modern slavery legislation. Vulnerable Polish nationals, including homeless people, former prisoners and people with alcohol dependency, were lured to England with offers of work, free or subsidised accommodation, food and travel, then put to work on farms, in recycling centres, poultry factories and parcel warehouses while wages were paid into gang-controlled bank accounts; some received as little as £10 a week. Police estimated up to 400 people were exploited and the gang earned more than £2 million. Bank cards and identity documents were confiscated and threats and violence used to stop people leaving. On 5 July 2019 Birmingham Crown Court sentenced Ignacy Brzezinski to 11 years, Wojciech Nowakowski to six and a half years and Jan Sadowski to three years, following convictions of five others in an earlier trial.
